title: In a graph that started as a tree with n nodes and had one extra edge added, return the edge that creates a cycle (if multiple, return the last one in input order).
shortTitle: Redundant Connection — detect the cycle edge via Union-Find

s1_definition.profdef: Process edges in input order and union their endpoints; the first edge whose two endpoints already share a root is the redundant edge that closes a cycle. Because the input is a tree plus exactly one extra edge, there is exactly one such edge, and returning it as encountered satisfies the "last in input order" tie-break.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wires branches into a tree so every branch is reachable without loops. One extra cable was mistakenly laid, creating a loop. You lay cables one by one; the cable that connects two branches already reachable from each other is the redundant one, and you flag it for removal.
s1_definition.oneliner: The redundant edge is the first edge whose endpoints are already connected — find(u) equals find(v) before you union.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Process edges in input order and union their endpoints; the first edge whose two endpoints already share a root is the redundant edge that closes a cycle. Because the input is a tree plus exactly one extra edge, there is exactly one such edge, and returning it as encountered satisfies the "last in input order" tie-break.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wires branches into a tree so every branch is reachable without loops. One extra cable was mistakenly laid, creating a loop. You lay cables one by one; the cable that connects two branches already reachable from each other is the redundant one, and you flag it for removal.

**One line to remember:** The redundant edge is the first edge whose endpoints are already connected — find(u) equals find(v) before you union.

sections.s2_technical:
Initialize Union-Find over the nodes (one-indexed here). For each edge, check whether its endpoints already share a root; if so, that edge is redundant. For example: `if (find(u) == find(v)) return edge; else union(u, v);`.

Because the graph is a tree with one added edge, exactly one edge will fail the union test, and since you scan in input order, the one you return is the last such edge in the input, satisfying the problem's tie-break rule.

The time is the number of edges times the near-constant union cost, and the space is the parent array. A senior nuance is that this generalizes to cycle detection in any undirected graph built incrementally, and that for the directed variant (Redundant Connection II) you additionally track in-degree-two conflicts, which is a different, harder problem.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the inter-branch settlement topology must be a tree so there are no routing loops. A misconfiguration added one extra link, creating a loop that causes duplicate settlement messages. This is exactly how the redundant-connection problem works.

Problem 2 — Operations must identify precisely which link to remove to restore the tree. This is exactly the edge that joins two already-connected branches.

The mini-project builds a `RedundantLinkFinder`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three links among three branches.

Step 1: Union-Find starts with branches one, two, three each their own root.

Step 2: Link one-two unions successfully, joining branches one and two.

Step 3: Link one-three unions successfully, pulling branch three into the same network.

Step 4: Link two-three is examined; both already share a root, so this edge closes a cycle and is the redundant link.

Step 5: The finder returns two-three as the link to remove, restoring the tree.

2026-10-26T23:20:00Z [SEVERE] Redundant link detected: 2-3

```

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Redundant Connection is a textbook application of Union-Find for cycle detection. The graph began as a tree and had exactly one extra edge added, so I process edges in their input order and, for each one, check whether its two endpoints already belong to the same set before unioning them. The moment I find an edge whose endpoints already share a root, that edge is the one that closes a cycle, and it is the edge I return.

Scanning in input order matters because the problem asks for the last redundant edge when several candidates exist, and since the input is a tree plus one edge there is precisely one offending edge, so returning it as I encounter it is correct. The whole thing runs in near-linear time using just a parent array.

In my project at National Bank of India, the inter-branch settlement topology was supposed to be a loop-free tree, but a misconfiguration added one extra link that caused duplicate settlement messages to circulate. I used this exact approach to pinpoint the offending link: the first link whose two branches were already reachable from one another was flagged for removal, which restored the tree and stopped the duplicates.
